sentences.text: The animal is classified under the genus Phosphatodraco, with the type species Phosphatodraco mauritanicus described by Pereda-Suberbiola and colleagues in 2003.
The genus is based on the holotype specimen OCP DEK/GE 111, an individual that may have had a wingspan of nearly five meters.
This large azhdarchid pterosaur lived in what is now Morocco during the Late Cretaceous, with researchers estimating its wingspan at approximately 5 meters.

The preserved cervical vertebrae have hollow centers with an outer bone layer approximately 1 millimeter thick, and the longest preserved vertebra, identified as C5, was estimated to be about 300 millimeters long when complete.

Phosphatodraco is distinguished by a very elongated C8 (or C7) vertebra that is 50% longer than the C5 and a prominent neural spine almost as tall as the centrum, though Kellner's reinterpretation shifted the order of these vertebrae to C3 through C8.
Phosphatodraco was one of the last pterosaurs to live just before the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction ended the group.
During preparation of the specimen, fossil remains of fish and mosasaurs were found in association with the pterosaur bones.
A specimen consisting of five cervical vertebrae was discovered in the Ouled Abdoun Phosphatic Basin in 2000 by the Office Chérifien des Phosphates near Khouribga in central Morocco.

It is debated whether azhdarchids like Phosphatodraco were skim-feeders in coastal waters or terrestrial foragers like storks or ground hornbills, as some researchers point to marine fossil contexts and the lack of finds in truly terrestrial strata.

Witton and Naish argued that azhdarchids likely inhabited inland environments and acted as terrestrial stalkers, using long limbs and stiffened necks to spot and grab small animals or fruit from the ground despite their small, pad-footed feet being unsuited for wading.

Azhdarchids are the only pterosaur group for which trackways have been identified, such as Haenamichnus from Korea, and Witton suggested that while they could likely launch from water, they were not as proficient swimmers as other pterosaur groups.
It is debated whether azhdarchids were adapted solely for soaring or if their musculature allowed them to flap their wings like swans and geese.

In 2003, researchers classified Phosphatodraco as an azhdarchid based on elongated cervical vertebrae with low or absent neural spines and specific skull features similar to Quetzalcoatlus and Azhdarcho, and a 2018 study found it to be the closest relative to Aralazhdarcho from Kazakhstan.
Mark Witton grouped Phosphatodraco with midsized azhdarchids in 2013 based on size estimates.
Phosphatodraco lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.

The Late Cretaceous of Morocco holds the most diverse pterosaur assemblage known, including Phosphatodraco, Pteranodontidae, and Nyctosauridae, and the sediments containing Phosphatodraco were deposited in an embayment of the eastern Atlantic Ocean that flooded North Africa during the Late Cretaceous and Early Paleogene.

The diversity of pterosaurs including Phosphatodraco in the late Maastrichtian suggests their extinction happened abruptly 66 million years ago, and researchers suggest the extinction of pterosaurs was abrupt due to the Chicxulub impact, which allowed birds to rapidly evolve and fill their niches.

There is controversy over the order of the fragmentary holotype cervical vertebrae, as researchers originally interpreted the five preserved neck vertebrae as vertebrae C5 through C9, and some suggest the last two vertebrae might be dorsal vertebrae that have been incorporated into the neck, a phenomenon known as cervicalization.
